relationships.relationship: UAP/UFO report counts x regional seismic activity over time (Tectonic Strain Theory: monthly or yearly report counts vs earthquake counts, magnitudes or seismic energy, with lags)
relationships.summary: This is the core claim of Persinger and Lafreniere's Tectonic Strain Theory (TST; book 1977, many papers 1975-2001). Nearly all supporting work comes from one group (Persinger, Derr) in Perceptual and Motor Skills, and the reported effects are large. Uinta Basin (Utah, 1967): monthly UFO reports correlated r = 0.80 with the summed earthquake magnitudes within 150 km, strongest in the same month. Carman, Manitoba (1974-77): monthly reports said to track seismic energy released within 1000 km, judged by visual inspection. Zeitoun (Egypt) luminous 'apparitions' (1968-69): r = 0.56 with seismicity, with the lights preceding a tenfold rise in seismicity about 400 km away. A companion paper reports that geomagnetic variability 'enhances' UFO reports only while tectonic strain is rising; the association weakens when earthquake variance is held constant. Critiques: Rutkowski (1984 thesis) says the analysis has too many degrees of freedom. The radius was widened from near the epicentre out to 150-1000 km, the lag was allowed to scale with magnitude, and small events were included, so the theory can hardly be falsified. He also notes that a bigger radius brings in more population, and that flap years are worldwide and do not follow local seismicity. Persinger replied in 1985 by pointing to multivariate consistency across regions. I found no independent replication using modern earthquake catalogs (ANSS ComCat) and large report databases (NUFORC, Hatch, GEIPAN) with controls for population and reporting trends. The claimed effects come from small samples chosen after the fact, and there is no out-of-sample prediction.

references.citation: Persinger MA, Derr JS (1985). Geophysical variables and behavior: XXIII. Relations between UFO reports within the Uinta Basin and local seismicity. Perceptual and Motor Skills 60(1):143-152. PMID 3982923
references.finding: Monthly UFO reports correlated r = 0.80 with the summed monthly earthquake magnitudes within 150 km; strongest in the same month. Read as support for moving strain fields.

references.citation: Persinger MA (1985). Geophysical variables and behavior: XXXII. Evaluations of UFO reports in an area of infrequent seismicity: the Carman, Manitoba episode. Perceptual and Motor Skills 61(3):807ff
references.finding: Monthly UFO reports for 1974-77 judged by visual inspection to be strongly correlated with seismic energy released within 1000 km.

references.citation: Derr JS, Persinger MA (1989). Geophysical variables and behavior: LIV. Zeitoun (Egypt) apparitions of the Virgin Mary as tectonic strain-induced luminosities. Perceptual and Motor Skills 68(1):123-128. DOI 10.2466/pms.1989.68.1.123
references.finding: Correlation of 0.56 between seismicity and luminous displays; the displays came before a tenfold rise in seismicity about 400 km away.

references.citation: Persinger MA (1985). Geophysical variables and behavior: XXI. Geomagnetic variation as possible enhancement stimuli for UFO reports preceding earthtremors. Perceptual and Motor Skills 60(1):37-38. PMID 3982943 (Europe PMC record query)
references.finding: Geomagnetic variability linked to UFO reports only while tectonic strain is rising; the association weakens when earthquake variance is held constant. This is a claimed interaction term.

references.citation: Rutkowski CA (1984). The Tectonic Strain Theory of Geophysical Luminosities (geophysical thesis, Winnipeg; ASCII version posted 1994)
references.finding: Critique: flexible radius (up to 200-1000 km) and magnitude-dependent lags leave the theory with no predictive power. Population confounding (larger radius means more observers). Manitoba flap years (1952, 1967, 1975) match worldwide flaps but no local earthquakes.

references.citation: Persinger MA (1985). Geophysical variables and behavior: XXVI. A response to Rutkowski's critique of the tectonic strain hypothesis for UFO phenomena. Perceptual and Motor Skills 60(2):575-582. PMID 4000876
references.finding: Reply arguing that multivariate and bivariate analyses show systematic UFO-report and earthquake relationships across several regions and periods.

relationships.relationship: UAP report locations x proximity to geological faults or seismically active zones (spatial association)
relationships.summary: The claim is old. Fernand Lagarde (Lumieres Dans La Nuit #92, 1968) mapped the 1954 French landing cases against geological faults. Devereux (Earth Lights, 1982; Earth Lights Revelation, 1989) and Persinger built the 'earth lights near faults' idea on it. Derr and Persinger (1986, Experientia) linked nocturnal lights in southern Washington (the Yakima area) to minor earthquakes, especially when epicentres moved across active compressional faults. Counter-evidence: Rutkowski (1984) found that Manitoba's 500+ reports (150+ locations) follow rural population density, not faults, in an essentially aseismic province. Van Utrecht (2007) points to selection bias (researchers looking for cases near faults) and finds no demonstrated link to epicentres. Medina et al. (2023, Sci Rep; NUFORC 2001-2020) show that sky-view and air-traffic covariates explain spatial variation in US reports. That makes population, sky darkness and air traffic mandatory confounders, although their study did not test faults or seismicity. One unrefereed 2023-24 claim (Kovalyov, CREDO workshop) says US UAP and seismicity maps look 'astoundingly' similar. It is a visual comparison with no confounder control. I found no peer-reviewed, confounder-controlled spatial test (for example, distance to mapped Quaternary faults with matched population and land-cover controls) on NUFORC, Hatch or GEIPAN data.

references.citation: Gross P. (n.d.) France 1954 case page, Niort, October 1954, quoting F. Lagarde's fault map from Lumieres Dans La Nuit #92 (Jan 1968)
references.finding: Documents Lagarde's 1968 claim of a link between 1954 landing sites and geological faults or earthquakes. Gross says the idea was 'essentially wrong'; no statistical test.

references.citation: Derr J, Persinger M (1986). Luminous phenomena and earthquakes in southern Washington. Experientia 42(9):991-999
references.finding: Nocturnal lights associated with very small earthquakes; said to occur when the locus of seismicity moves across an active fault under compressional stress.

references.citation: Rutkowski CA (1984). The Tectonic Strain Theory of Geophysical Luminosities (thesis)
references.finding: Manitoba report distribution matches rural population density; only about 8 earthquakes within 200 km of the border in 100 years; a fault-UFO link 'appears geographically untenable'.

references.citation: van Utrecht W. (2007). A note on Earth(Quake) Lights. CAELESTIA
references.finding: Fault-proximity claims show selection bias; no demonstrated epicentre-location link and no statistical evidence that sighting dates line up with seismic periods.

references.citation: Medina RM, Brewer SC, Kirkpatrick SM (2023). An environmental analysis of public UAP sightings and sky view potential. Scientific Reports. DOI 10.1038/s41598-023-49527-x
references.finding: In about 98,000 US NUFORC reports (2001-2020), light pollution (-7.7% per SD), tree canopy, airports and military area explain spatial variation; cloud cover not credible. Seismicity and faults were not tested.

references.citation: Kovalyov M. (2024). On the relationship between seismic activity and other natural phenomena. 1st CREDO Visegrad Workshop (abstract)
references.finding: Unrefereed talk claiming that quakes correlate with UAPs, using the Medina et al. 2023 UAP distribution. Visual comparison only; no confounder control.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x short spatiotemporal windows around moderate-to-large (M>=5) earthquakes, especially intraplate rift or subvertical-fault settings (earthquake-light-type stimulus)
relationships.summary: Outside UAP research, earthquake lights (EQL) are an established phenomenon in seismology, now backed by documented cases and video. Theriault et al. (2014, SRL) compiled 65 well-documented EQL cases from the Americas and Europe since 1600. They found 85% spatially on or near rifts and 97% next to subvertical faults (rift, graben, strike-slip or transform), although such settings produce only about 5% of global seismicity. About 80% were with M>=5, and lights appeared before or during the mainshock, not after. Kato (Kyoto) objected that intraplate events often hit populated regions, so observation bias was not handled. Fidani (2010) catalogued L'Aquila 2009 luminous reports from about 9 months before to 5 months after the shock, up to about 50 km north. Whitehead and Ulusoy (2023) analysed more than 700 flashes in 127+ videos from the 2023 M7.8/M7.6 Turkey quakes. Median duration was 0.3 s, they found no evidence of grid failure, and they saw no predictive value. The Condon Report (Altschuler, ch. 7) already listed earthquake luminescence as a possible UFO stimulus but drew no firm link. Persinger tested monthly aggregates, not event windows. I found no study that does an event-level test of UAP databases (NUFORC, Hatch, GEIPAN) against a modern catalog, using hours-to-days windows around M>=5 events, setting covariates (rift or subvertical fault) and matched control windows. The geophysics predicts short, mostly co-seismic flashes that should cluster tightly in time, which is a sharp and testable signature.

references.citation: Theriault R, St-Laurent F, Freund FT, Derr JS (2014). Prevalence of Earthquake Lights Associated with Rift Environments. Seismological Research Letters 85(1):159-178. DOI 10.1785/0220130059
references.finding: 65 EQL cases: 85% on or near rifts, 97% next to subvertical faults (about 5% of global seismicity); mostly M>=5; lights before or during, not after, the mainshock.

references.citation: Physics World (2014). Study homes in on the cause of earthquake lights (news report including independent critique by M. Kato)
references.finding: Kato: the Theriault et al. analysis 'appears to fail to take this sampling bias into account' (intraplate quakes often strike populated areas); 'premature in its conclusions'.

references.citation: Fidani C (2010). The earthquake lights (EQL) of the 6 April 2009 Aquila earthquake, in Central Italy. Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences 10:967-978
references.finding: Seven-month testimony catalogue: luminous phenomena reported from about 9 months before to 5 months after the mainshock, spread up to about 50 km, tied to landscape and source features.

references.citation: Whitehead NE, Ulusoy U (2023). New Contributions to Understanding Earthquake Light, from the 2023 Turkish Earthquakes. 7th Int. Conf. on Earthquake Engineering and Seismology, Antalya
references.finding: More than 700 flashes in 127+ videos; median duration 0.3 s; mostly white or blue; no evidence of grid-failure origin; not useful for prediction.

references.citation: Altschuler MD (1969). Atmospheric Electricity and Plasma Interpretations of UFOs. Condon Report (Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects), Section VI, Chapter 7
references.finding: Reviews historical earthquake luminescence (fireballs, luminous clouds) as a possible UFO stimulus; draws no firm UFO connection.

relationships.relationship: Luminous aerial phenomena x crustal stress via stress-activated charge carriers (peroxy defects / positive holes) or piezoelectricity (physical mechanism behind TST and EQL)
relationships.summary: Two mechanisms have been proposed. The older one is piezoelectric (quartz) fields from seismic strain (Finkelstein and Powell 1970). The newer and leading one is Freund's peroxy-defect / positive-hole model: stress breaks peroxy bonds in igneous rocks, the mobile charge flows to the surface, ionises air and causes corona discharges and lights (Freund 2003, 2011; St-Laurent, Derr and Freund 2006). Lab work shows stress-stimulated currents in dry rock. But Dahlgren et al. (2014, BSSA), from a USGS-affiliated group, measured 50-400 pA transients in dry gabbro and none in brine-saturated gabbro, which is closer to real fault zones. Rutkowski (1984) estimated energy budgets: piezoelectric emission of about 1e-15 W against roughly 60 W for a visible light ball at 100 m, plus signal loss through rock. The ICEF report (Jordan et al. 2011) found that no electromagnetic or other precursor has produced a successful short-term prediction scheme. Freund et al. (2017) admit that precursor reports are intermittent and call for systematic statistical testing. Summary: the mechanism is plausible for brief co-seismic lights but has not been shown to make long-lived, UAP-like objects far from epicentres, which is the strong form TST needs.

references.citation: Freund F (2011). Pre-earthquake signals: Underlying physical processes. Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 41:383-400
references.finding: Stress-activated positive holes flow out of stressed rock, ionise air at the ground-air interface and can cause corona discharges and earthquake lights.

references.citation: St-Laurent F, Derr JS, Freund FT (2006). Earthquake lights and the stress-activation of positive hole charge carriers in rocks. Physics and Chemistry of the Earth 31(4-9):305-312
references.finding: Proposes that p-hole charge builds up at crustal weak points, escapes upward as a plasma, and makes corona discharge and light at the surface.

references.citation: Derr JS (1986). Luminous phenomena and their relationship to rock fracture. Nature 321(6069):470-471
references.finding: USGS seismologist's Nature commentary linking luminous phenomena to rock-fracture electrodynamics.

references.citation: Dahlgren RP, Johnston MJS, Vanderbilt VC, Nakaba RN (2014). Comparison of the stress-stimulated current of dry and fluid saturated gabbro samples. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America 104:2662-2672
references.finding: Dry gabbro: 50-400 pA stress-stimulated current transients. Brine-saturated gabbro: none, consistent with self-discharge. This challenges the field relevance of the mechanism.

references.citation: Jordan TH et al. (2011). Operational Earthquake Forecasting: State of Knowledge and Guidelines for Utilization (ICEF report). Annals of Geophysics 54(4). DOI 10.4401/ag-5350
references.finding: After reviewing EM, radon and other precursors: 'The search for diagnostic precursors has not yet produced a successful short-term prediction scheme.'

references.citation: Freund F, Ouillon G, Scoville J, Sornette D (2017). Earthquake precursors in the light of peroxy defects theory: critical review of systematic observations. arXiv:1711.01780
references.finding: Argues that peroxy-bond rupture underlies all precursors but admits the reports are intermittent and need rigorous continuous statistical testing.

relationships.relationship: Recurrent fixed-site light phenomena (Hessdalen-type 'earth lights') x local geology, radon, geomagnetic activity
relationships.summary: Hessdalen (Norway) is the best-instrumented recurring light site: 15-20 events per week in 1981-84, now 10-20 per year. It has optical spectra, radar returns, and VLF/HF pulses, and the lights occur independently of thunderstorms. Proposed geophysical mechanisms include combustion of valley dust containing scandium (Hauge 2007, 2010), a dusty plasma of Coulomb crystals ionised by alpha particles from radon decay (Paiva and Taft 2010, JASTP), piezoelectricity from rock strain (Paiva and Taft), and a valley-scale 'natural battery' of zinc and copper slopes with an acidic river as electrolyte (Monari et al. 2013). Physicist Bjorn Samset judged the battery currents and distances far too weak for the observed brightness. Project Hessdalen ran a seismograph in 1984-85, but its 30-year summary at a GEIPAN workshop reports no seismic correlation. It notes only that lights were 'easier to see' when magnetic activity and humidity were high, and that the day with most observations in a 1995 Australian Min Min expedition had high magnetic activity. Other 'hotspot' lights have been explained conventionally: the Min Min light as Fata Morgana refraction of distant sources (Pettigrew 2003), and many Marfa lights as distant car headlights confirmed by oxygen-band spectroscopy (Stephan and Ghimire). No mechanism is accepted, and I found no systematic, controlled test linking such sites to seismic strain.

references.citation: Strand E, Hauge BG, Zlotnicki J, Montebugnoli S, Monari J, Blank E, Farges T, Yvetot P, Fauquet F. The Hessdalen Phenomena, 30 years of research (GEIPAN/CNES workshop presentation)
references.finding: Instruments included a seismograph, magnetometer, radar and spectrum analyser. Lights seen on radar when not visible; 'easier to see... when there are high magnetic activity and humidity(?)'; no seismic result reported.

references.citation: Caron E, Faridi P (2016). To Investigate or Not to Investigate? Researchers' Views on Unexplored Atmospheric Light Phenomena. Frontiers in Earth Science 4:17. DOI 10.3389/feart.2016.00017
references.finding: Summarises the Hessdalen literature: about 19 kW luminosity, independent of thunderstorms. Competing models (scandium dust combustion, radon dusty plasma, geological battery); none explains all observations.

references.citation: Paiva GS, Taft CA (2010). A hypothetical dusty plasma mechanism of Hessdalen lights. Journal of Atmospheric and Solar-Terrestrial Physics 72(16):1200-1203
references.finding: Lights proposed as Coulomb crystals in a dusty plasma ionised by alpha particles from radon decay; accounts for oscillation, geometry and spectrum.

references.citation: ScienceNorway (2014). Little valley - a giant battery? (reporting Monari, Montebugnoli, Serra 2013, with comment by physicist B. Samset)
references.finding: Zinc and copper valley sides plus a sulphur-acid river make a natural battery. Critic: distances too large and charge too weak to explain the brightness.

references.citation: University of Queensland News (2003). UQ scientist unlocks secret of Min Min lights (reporting Pettigrew JD, Clinical and Experimental Optometry 86(2):109-120, DOI 10.1111/j.1444-0938.2003.tb03069.x)
references.finding: The Min Min light is natural or man-made light refracted to observers tens to hundreds of km away by an inverted mirage (Fata Morgana): a conventional optical explanation for a 'hotspot' light.

references.citation: Ghimire S (2010; with KD Stephan). Spectroscopic Measurements of Natural and Artificial Light Sources (Texas State University thesis, Marfa lights)
references.finding: 20-night spectroscopic study at Marfa; no 'true' Marfa light met all criteria; oxygen-band (760 nm) ranging showed candidate lights were distant headlights.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports (nocturnal lights, low-altitude glowing spheres) x thunderstorm/lightning activity via ball lightning
relationships.summary: Philip Klass proposed in the 1960s that plasma or ball lightning explains many UFO reports, including aircraft encounters. The Condon Report (Altschuler, ch. 7) accepted ball lightning as a genuine electrical effect and saw similarities with the Exeter reports. It also found that confining a plasma beyond about 1 s in air is unlikely, attributed no Blue Book case to it, and noted that other seacoast towns with similar conditions had no UFO wave. Since then ball lightning has been firmly established outside UAP research. Cen, Yuan and Xue (2014, PRL) recorded the first spectrum of natural ball lightning: about 5 m across, about 1.6 s long, moving about 8.6 m/s, with Si, Fe and Ca soil emission lines. This supports the Abrahamson and Dinniss (2000, Nature) model of soil nanoparticle oxidation. Rayle (1966, NASA TN D-3188) used a survey to compare how often people saw ball lightning with how often they saw ordinary strike points. Peer and Kendl (2010) suggested lightning EMP could induce phosphenes, which would make some ball-lightning reports perceptual rather than physical; their erratum later concluded cortical stimulation is unlikely and retinal stimulation more likely. Ball lightning is rare, short-lived and tied to cloud-to-ground strokes, so it predicts UAP reports clustered within minutes and a few km of CG lightning. I found no statistical test of UAP databases against lightning-detection data (for example NLDN flash density or storm days).

references.citation: Altschuler MD (1969). Atmospheric Electricity and Plasma Interpretations of UFOs. Condon Report Section VI, Chapter 7
references.finding: Ball lightning is genuine, but no mechanism explains all reports. Plasma confinement beyond about 1 s in air is unlikely. Klass's Exeter plasma explanation is weakened because similar towns had no reports.

references.citation: Cen J, Yuan P, Xue S (2014). Observation of the Optical and Spectral Characteristics of Ball Lightning. Physical Review Letters 112:035001
references.finding: Ball lightning from a CG stroke observed spectroscopically at 0.9 km: about 5 m, about 1.64 s, about 8.6 m/s horizontal; Si, Fe, Ca lines present throughout.

references.citation: Abrahamson J, Dinniss J (2000). Ball lightning caused by oxidation of nanoparticle networks from normal lightning strikes on soil. Nature 403:519-521
references.finding: Lab discharges into soil produce oxidising Si/SiO/SiC nanoparticle networks with lifetimes that fit ball lightning.

references.citation: Rayle WD (1966). Ball lightning characteristics. NASA Technical Note D-3188 (NASA Lewis Research Center)
references.finding: Survey comparing how often ball lightning was seen with how often ordinary lightning strike points were seen, plus brightness, size, duration and colour. Useful as a base rate.

references.citation: Peer J, Kendl A (2010). Transcranial stimulability of phosphenes by long lightning electromagnetic pulses. Physics Letters A, pp. 2932-2935 (arXiv:1005.1153, with erratum)
references.finding: Proposed that lightning EMP induces phosphenes as one reading of luminous perceptions in storms. The erratum lowers the field estimates: cortical stimulation unlikely, retinal phosphenes more plausible.

relationships.relationship: Luminous/UFO report counts x precipitation or hydrological loading (rainfall-modulated crustal strain)
relationships.summary: Derr and Persinger (2001) reported that over 50% of the variance in yearly anomalous-luminosity reports in the San Francisco Basin (1950-69) was explained by January rainfall, with a threshold of about 8.5 inches. Effects were strongest within 100 km of cities. They read this as fluid loading changing crustal strain. In seismology, rainfall-triggered seismicity is established at some close-to-failure sites through pore-pressure diffusion (Hainzl et al. 2006, Mt Hochstaufen), so the physical link from rain to strain is real. But the step from rain to UAP is confounded: precipitation and cloud directly change sky visibility and observer behaviour. Notably, Medina et al. (2023) found no credible effect of cloud cover on US report rates. I found no replication of the rainfall-luminosity result. A rigorous test would need lagged precipitation with same-time weather and visibility controls, in regions with documented hydroseismicity.

references.citation: Derr JS, Persinger MA (2001). Geophysical variables and behavior: XCV. Annual January rainfall may modulate the incidence of luminous phenomena within the San Francisco Basin. Perceptual and Motor Skills 92(3 Pt 2):1180-1190
references.finding: >50% of the variance in yearly luminous-phenomena reports (1950-69) explained by January rainfall (threshold about 8.5 in); strongest within 100 km of cities.

references.citation: Hainzl S, Kraft T, Wassermann J, Igel H, Schmedes E (2006). Evidence for rainfall-triggered earthquake activity. Geophysical Research Letters 33
references.finding: Seismicity beneath Mt Hochstaufen is highly correlated with modelled pore-pressure changes from diffusing rainwater: an established rain-to-seismicity pathway at critically stressed sites.

references.citation: Medina RM, Brewer SC, Kirkpatrick SM (2023). An environmental analysis of public UAP sightings and sky view potential. Scientific Reports
references.finding: No credible relationship between cloud cover and US UAP report rates; visibility and air-traffic covariates matter. Weather and visibility must be controlled in any rainfall test.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x proximity to active volcanoes or eruptive activity (volcanic lightning, incandescent ejecta)
relationships.summary: I found no peer-reviewed or government study testing whether UAP report rates rise near active volcanoes or during eruptions. Evidence is anecdotal and media-driven (for example Popocatepetl webcam 'UFOs'). Patrick Gross reviewed hundreds of CENAPRED webcam images and found that close-range examples resolved as insects, with one luminous object possibly a firefly. Outside UAP research, volcanic lightning is well documented: McNutt and Williams (2010) catalogued it at 80 volcanoes in 212 explosive eruptions and related it to explosivity (VEI). That makes eruptions a plausible source of transient lights that could be reported as UAP. A testable relationship would be report excess within tens of km of eruptions with VEI>=2 (Smithsonian GVP dates) against matched non-eruption windows. I found no such test.

references.citation: McNutt SR, Williams ER (2010). Volcanic lightning: global observations and constraints on source mechanisms. Bulletin of Volcanology 72(10):1153-1167. DOI 10.1007/s00445-010-0393-4
references.finding: Volcanic lightning documented at 80 volcanoes in 212 explosive eruptions; occurrence related to eruption explosivity (VEI).

references.citation: Gross P. (n.d.). Popocatepetl volcano UFO photos analysis
references.finding: Hundreds of CENAPRED webcam 'UFO' images resolved as insects when the objects were closer; one 2000 luminous object possibly a firefly. No systematic volcano-UAP association shown.

relationships.relationship: Close-encounter / high-strangeness UAP experiences x strain-generated electromagnetic fields acting on the brain (temporal-lobe pathway), and associated health claims
relationships.summary: TST's second step says strain-related EM fields stimulate the temporal lobe and produce 'visitor' experiences, missing time and so on (Persinger 1989). Persinger (1988) also predicted more cancer and depression in UFO flap areas from EM and radon. Bisson and Persinger (1993) reported a male brain-tumour odds ratio of about 2.5 after the 1975 Sudbury Basin luminous displays, but within normal population ranges. Rutkowski and Del Bigio (1989, CMAJ) disputed the UFO-cancer claims. The key lab pillar, that weak (microtesla) complex fields evoke a sensed presence, failed independent double-blind replication: Granqvist et al. (2005, N = 89) found no field effect, and suggestibility (absorption, new-age orientation) predicted the reports. Report databases cannot test this directly, but TST predicts that high-strangeness or close-encounter categories should cluster more tightly with seismic proxies than distant lights do. I found no controlled test of that.

references.citation: Persinger MA (1989). Geophysical variables and behavior: LV. Predicting the details of visitor experiences and the personality of experients: the temporal lobe factor. Perceptual and Motor Skills 68(1):55-65; and Persinger MA (1988) LIII. Epidemiological considerations for incidence of cancer and depression in areas of frequent UFO reports, PMS 67(3):799-803 (Europe PMC records)
references.finding: Visitor experiences proposed to reflect temporal-lobe lability set off by tectonic strain fields; EM and radon in flap areas predicted to raise brain-tumour, leukaemia and depression rates.

references.citation: Bisson C, Persinger MA (1993). Geophysical variables and behavior: LXXV. Possible increased incidence of brain tumors following an episode of luminous phenomena. Perceptual and Motor Skills 77(3 Pt 2):1088-1090 (Europe PMC record)
references.finding: Sudbury Basin, after the 1975 luminous episode: conservative male brain-tumour odds ratio about 2.5, but within expected population ranges.

references.citation: Rutkowski CA, Del Bigio MR (1989). UFOs and cancer? Canadian Medical Association Journal 140(11):1258-1259. PMID 2720499
references.finding: Published letter disputing the proposed link between UFO-flap EM exposure (tectonic strain hypothesis) and cancer.

references.citation: Granqvist P, Fredrikson M, Unge P, Hagenfeldt A, Valind S, Larhammar D, Larsson M (2005). Sensed presence and mystical experiences are predicted by suggestibility, not by the application of transcranial weak complex magnetic fields. Neuroscience Letters 379(1):1-6
references.finding: Double-blind, sham-controlled (N = 89): no effect of weak complex magnetic fields; suggestibility traits predicted the experiences. A failed replication of TST's neuro pathway.

relationships.relationship: UAP report counts (annual, regional) x lagged geomagnetic activity indices (Persinger's tectonic-strain regression models)
relationships.summary: Persinger (1981) used multiple regression and reported that more than 80% of the variance in annual UFO report counts for the central and eastern USA in 1950-1966 was 'accommodated' by geomagnetic and seismic measures from the previous 1-3 years. The geomagnetic term was INVERSE and lagged: reports rose 2-3 years after DECREASES in geomagnetic activity, and the year after increases in local low-intensity earthquakes. A later New Madrid study (1952-1969) reported multiple R > 0.83 using 5-6 lagged solar-geomagnetic and seismic predictors. The Psi Encyclopedia says Persinger's model also accounted for about 80% of the 1967-1981 variation, but that claim is not independently verified. Critiques: Rutkowski (1984) objected to tiny counts (one analysis used 214 Fate-magazine reports over 15 years), lag searches over 1-6 years, square-root transforms and recoding of outliers (overfitting and forking paths), and an unmodelled population-density confound. Persinger published a rebuttal (1985). Medina et al. (2023) describe the tectonic-strain work as 'refuted soon after publication'. No independent replication against modern databases (NUFORC, GEIPAN, Hatch *U*, Blue Book) was located. Note that the claimed inverse, multi-year-lag sign is the opposite of what a simple aurora-misidentification mechanism predicts (a positive, same-night effect).

references.citation: Persinger, M.A. (1981). Geophysical variables and behavior: III. Prediction of UFO reports by geomagnetic and seismic activity. Perceptual and Motor Skills 53(1):115-122. doi:10.2466/pms.1981.53.1.115
references.finding: Over 80% of the variance in annual UFO report numbers (central/eastern USA, 1950-1966) explained by geomagnetic/seismic measures lagged 1-3 years; reports rose 2-3 years after decreases in geomagnetic activity (inverse relation).

references.citation: Persinger, M.A. (1983). Geophysical variables and human behavior: VIII. Specific prediction of UFO reports within the New Madrid States by solar-geomagnetic and seismic measures. Perceptual and Motor Skills 56:243-249. doi:10.2466/pms.1983.56.1.243
references.finding: 1952-1969 data for six states near New Madrid: optimal equations with multiple R > 0.83 using 5-6 lagged solar-geomagnetic and seismic variables 'predicted' UFO flaps; predictions issued for 1970-1982.

references.citation: Rutkowski, C.A. (1984). The Tectonic Strain Theory of Geophysical Luminosities (geophysical thesis, Winnipeg; ASCII version circulated 1994)
references.finding: Methodological critique: very small yearly counts, predictors lagged 1-6 years, square-root transforms of sunspot numbers, outlier recoding, larger search radii that also enlarge the reporting population. Manitoba UFO report distribution closely follows rural population distribution.

references.citation: Persinger, M.A. (1985). Geophysical variables and behavior: XXVI. A response to Rutkowski's critique of the tectonic strain hypothesis for UFO phenomena. Perceptual and Motor Skills 60(2):575-582. doi:10.2466/pms.1985.60.2.575
references.finding: Persinger's rebuttal to Rutkowski; it documents that the statistical critique was raised in the peer-reviewed record.

references.citation: Psi Encyclopedia (Society for Psychical Research). Michael A. Persinger (encyclopedia entry)
references.finding: Summarises Persinger's claim that 1950-1966 UFO reports showed an inverse relation with geomagnetic activity and a positive relation with tectonic strain, and that 80% of the temporal variation in 1967-1981 was accounted for (secondary, sympathetic source).

references.citation: Medina, R.M., Brewer, S.C., Kirkpatrick, S.M. (2023). An environmental analysis of public UAP sightings and sky view potential. Scientific Reports 13. PMC10721628
references.finding: Modern NUFORC-based Bayesian study (about 98,000 US reports, 2001-2020) used light pollution, cloud cover, tree canopy, airports and military areas but NO space-weather covariates; describes the tectonic-strain/geomagnetic work as refuted soon after publication.

relationships.relationship: UAP sightings x short-timescale (daily/hourly) geomagnetic disturbance, including local magnetogram disturbances, storm days and instrumented recurrent luminous phenomena (Hessdalen, Min-Min)
relationships.summary: Poher (1974) and Poher & Vallee (1975, AIAA 75-42) compared French October 1954 wave reports with the Chambon-la-Foret magnetograms. For 1-18 October they reported r = 0.58 between daily UFO observations and disturbances in the vertical field component, and r = 0.034 for declination. They interpreted this as UFOs CAUSING the disturbances, not as a space-weather driver, and used n of about 18 days with no autocorrelation control. Persinger (1985, XXI) found that in six-month New Madrid windows the geomagnetic-variability/UFO association 'deteriorated' once shared variance with earthquakes was controlled. At Hessdalen, Strand (EGU 2011) reported that 40% of sightings occurred during a magnetic pulsation and that 'a magnetic storm seems to increase the probability for a sighting'. No base rate of pulsations or control for observer effort was given. A 1995 Australian Min-Min light expedition noted high magnetic activity on the day with the most observations. Persinger et al. (1996) analysed a 'strobe-light' luminosity filmed during a 1994 geomagnetic storm. Recent instrumentation (Galileo Project magnetometer; MADAR/NUFORC 'Project Match') targets co-located field anomalies but publishes no rate statistics. A 2026 arXiv preprint reports a monotonic Kp dose-response (17.4% at quiet Kp down to 2.4% at Kp 8-9) for POSS-I plate transients. That dataset is UAP-adjacent and contested, and it is not witness reports. No daily event study of NUFORC/MUFON/GEIPAN/Hatch report rates versus Kp, Ap, Dst or AE storm days was located.

references.citation: Poher, C. & Vallee, J. (1975). Basic Patterns in UFO Observations. AIAA 13th Aerospace Sciences Meeting, paper 75-42 (cites Poher, C. 1974, 'Time correlations between geomagnetic disturbances and eye-witness accounts of UFOs', Flying Saucer Review 20(1):12-16)
references.finding: Oct 1-18, 1954 French reports vs Chambon-la-Foret magnetograms: r = 0.58 with vertical-component disturbances, r = 0.034 with declination; authors infer UFO-induced fields of about 10 gamma at 40 km.

references.finding: Correlations among earthquakes, UFO reports and geomagnetic variability in the New Madrid region weakened substantially once earthquake variance was controlled; geomagnetic variability 'may enhance' reports only when tectonic strain is increasing.

relationships.relationship: UAP report counts x solar activity (sunspot number / 11-year solar cycle / solar flares)
relationships.summary: The only located UAP-specific tests are Persinger's 1983 discriminant and regression analyses. In study VII, functions built from solar and seismic variables classified 19th-century (1849-1926) European 'luminosity' years with >90% accuracy and also 'forecast' 1945-1971 UFO report years. In study VIII, lagged solar-geomagnetic variables were included in the New Madrid predictions. The direction of the solar term is not stated in the abstracts. Rutkowski (1984) notes these analyses used years with fewer than 3 reports, lags of 1-6 years and square-root-transformed sunspot numbers. He also notes that the historical 'luminosity' series included accounts of 'phantom armies' in the sky, a classic historical description of aurora. This suggests (as our inference) that any solar association in pre-1947 data could partly be auroral misreporting. A closely analogous non-UAP test, Barry (1979) on ball lightning reports from 1651-1978, found NO positive correlation with solar activity and attributed structure in the record to publication bias, misidentification and changing public interest. No study of NUFORC, Hatch *U*, NICAP, GEIPAN or Blue Book counts versus sunspot number, F10.7 or flare indices was located. Any modern UAP database spans only about 2-7 solar cycles (NUFORC's online era about 2.5), so the effective sample for a cycle-scale test is tiny.

references.citation: Persinger, M.A. (1983). Geophysical variables and behavior: VII. Prediction of recent European UFO report years by nineteenth century luminosity and solar-seismic measures. Perceptual and Motor Skills 56:91-95. doi:10.2466/pms.1983.56.1.91
references.finding: Discriminant functions using solar and seismic variables classified 1849-1926 European luminosity years with >90% accuracy and also predicted 1945-1971 UFO report years.

references.citation: Persinger, M.A. (1983). Geophysical variables and human behavior: VIII. Specific prediction of UFO reports within the New Madrid States by solar-geomagnetic and seismic measures. Perceptual and Motor Skills 56:243-249
references.finding: Lagged solar-geomagnetic and seismic predictors, multiple R > 0.83, for 1952-1969 UFO reports.

references.citation: Rutkowski, C.A. (1984). The Tectonic Strain Theory of Geophysical Luminosities
references.finding: Sunspot numbers were square-root transformed against about 214 reports over 15 years; historical series had years with fewer than 3 reports and included 'phantom armies in the sky' accounts; solar and seismic variables were lagged 1-6 years.

references.citation: Barry, J.D. (1979). Frequency of ball lightning reports. Journal of Geophysical Research 84(C1):308. doi:10.1029/JC084iC01p00308
references.finding: Ball lightning reports and papers from 1651-1978 showed no positive correlation with solar activity; human factors (publication bias, misidentification, reporting hesitancy) likely shape the series.

relationships.relationship: Aurora (including low-latitude aurora during severe G4-G5 storms and STEVE/SAR arcs) as a misidentification source for UAP reports
relationships.summary: As a qualitative identified-object (IFO) category, aurora is long established. GEIPAN's case 'Aurore Boreale (975)' (13 March 1989, the great geomagnetic storm) had multiple French witnesses in Morbihan and Yvelines reporting a large multicoloured luminous phenomenon. SEPRA classified it B (probable natural phenomenon) and linked it to the contemporaneous solar eruption. The Condon Report's field cases include one (1321-B) in which an aurora display was in progress, but the aurora was not analysed as a cause. Outside UAP work, Spanish newspaper records show that low-latitude aurorae in 1957 and 1991 were reported to fire brigades as large fires, so lay misidentification at mid-latitudes is documented. STEVE, a sub-auroral optical structure, was only characterised in 2018 after citizen scientists flagged it, so earlier reports of such arcs would have lacked a known identification. In the May 2024 G5 storm, millions were alerted by smartphones and social media and 696 citizen-science aurora reports came from over 30 countries. That points to a storm-driven sky-watching surge (observer effort) that could inflate reports of anything in the sky, not only aurora. Gap: no study quantifying the storm-night excess of NUFORC, MUFON or GEIPAN reports, or its latitude dependence, was located. The quantitative version is effectively NO DIRECT PRECEDENT LOCATED.

references.citation: GEIPAN (CNES). Case 'Aurore Boreale' (975), Saint-Pierre-Quiberon (56) / Bennecourt (78), 13.03.1989 - Notes d'enquete (re-examined 2013)
references.finding: Multi-witness luminous phenomenon on the evening of the 13 March 1989 great storm, classified B (probable spectacular natural light phenomenon) and connected to the concurrent solar eruption. Details come from the search-result summary; direct PDF fetch was rate-limited.

references.finding: Case 1321-B notes 'a display of Aurora Borealis was in progress'; aurora is mentioned as context only, not evaluated as a cause.

references.finding: Low-latitude aurorae (1957, 1991) were reported to fire brigades as fires: documented lay misidentification of storm-time aurora at mid-latitudes.

references.citation: MacDonald, E.A. et al. (2018). New science in plain sight: Citizen scientists lead to the discovery of optical structure in the upper atmosphere. Science Advances (University of Calgary news release)
references.finding: STEVE, a mauve sub-auroral arc, was only scientifically characterised in 2018 after amateur reports, so before then a real luminous sky phenomenon had no standard identification.

references.finding: 696 citizen reports from 30+ countries; aurora seen at 30-60 degrees geomagnetic latitude; millions alerted via smartphones and social media, implying a large storm-driven increase in sky-watching effort.

references.finding: Notes that the historical 'UFO/luminosity' series used in solar-seismic correlations included 'phantom armies in the sky', a historical aurora trope, so aurora may contaminate historical UFO series.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports (especially radar/electronic and radar-visual cases) x ionospheric disturbance (sporadic-E, storm-time ionospheric irregularities, radar aurora, solar radio bursts)
relationships.summary: No study relating UAP report frequency to ionospheric indices (foF2, foEs, TEC, ionospheric storms) was located. The Condon Report's radar analysis treated anomalous propagation only as a tropospheric (refractivity/ducting) problem and did not evaluate ionospheric or auroral effects. In non-UAP radar engineering and space physics the link between ionospheric disturbance and false or ambiguous radar returns is well established. Radar aurora was studied from the 1950s precisely so that early-warning radars would not confuse aurora with ICBMs. On 23 May 1967 an extreme solar radio burst and geomagnetic/ionospheric storm disrupted polar surveillance radars, and the USAF initially interpreted this as Soviet jamming. Sporadic-E layers cause anomalous long-distance propagation of VHF (98-118 MHz) aeronautical navigation signals, confirmed against ionosonde data. Applying these mechanisms to radar UAP report rates (e.g., Blue Book radar cases, AARO radar cases) would therefore be a new test.

references.citation: Knipp, D.J., Ramsay, A.C., Beard, E.D., Boright, A.L., Cade, W.B., Hewins, I.M., McFadden, R., Denig, W.F., Kilcommons, L.M., Shea, M.A., Smart, D.F. (2016). The May 1967 great storm and radio disruption event: Extreme space weather and extraordinary responses. Space Weather. doi:10.1002/2016SW001423 (UCAR news summary)
references.finding: Solar radio burst and geomagnetic/ionospheric storm disrupted polar surveillance radars; the USAF prepared aircraft believing the radars were being jammed until space-weather forecasters identified the solar cause.

references.citation: SRI International. Atmospheric research and radar (history of radar-aurora research)
references.finding: Cold War radar-aurora research was needed so that US early-warning radars could distinguish Soviet ICBMs from natural aurora, i.e., aurora was a known false-target source.

references.citation: Network observation of anomalous long-distance propagation of aeronautical VHF navigation signals due to sporadic-E. Earth, Planets and Space (July 2020), doi:10.1186/s40623-020-01216-z (author list not verified)
references.finding: Sporadic-E caused anomalous long-distance VHF (98-118 MHz: VOR, ILS, GBAS) propagation, confirmed against ionosonde foEs > 15 MHz on 4 July 2019.

references.citation: Thayer, G.D. (1968). Optical and Radar Analyses of Field Cases. Condon Report, Section III, Chapter 5
references.finding: Radar UFO cases analysed only for tropospheric anomalous propagation (inversions, ducting); ionospheric, auroral and solar effects were not considered.

relationships.relationship: Solar activity -> thermospheric density/drag -> satellite and rocket-body reentry rate -> fireball-like UAP reports (mediated solar-cycle confound); plus geomagnetic storms causing prompt reentries
relationships.summary: Each link is well documented separately, but no study testing the full chain against UAP report counts was located. Link 1: high solar activity heats and expands the thermosphere, causing a 'dramatic increase in space object reentries' near solar maximum (NASA Orbital Debris chief scientist, 2012). Debris decay rates rise sharply when sunspot number exceeds 67-75% of the cycle peak, and EUV forcing dominates over geomagnetic indices on long timescales (Ashruf et al. 2026). Storms also act promptly: after the 3-4 February 2022 storms, 38 of 49 newly launched Starlink satellites reentered. Link 2: reentries and satellite trains generate UFO report clusters. Examples are a falling Orbital satellite reported as a UFO in South America, and the association between Starlink launch timing and the 2020 increase in NUFORC/MUFON reports (Cockrell, Murphy, Rodeghier). So any solar-cycle signal in UAP counts may be partly mediated by man-made reentries. Reentry and satellite catalogues (e.g., Space-Track decay data) are a natural negative-control or adjustment covariate.

references.citation: Johnson, N.L. (2012). The effects of solar maximum on the Earth's satellite population and space situational awareness. IAC-12.A6.2.9, NASA Orbital Debris Program Office
references.finding: 'The best known consequence of high solar activity is an increase in the density of the thermosphere... most prominent evidence... a dramatic increase in space object reentries.'

references.citation: Ashruf, A.M., Bhaskar, A., Vineeth, C., Pant, T.K. (2026). Characterizing solar cycle influence on long-term orbital deterioration of low-earth orbiting space debris. Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences 13. doi:10.3389/fspas.2026.1797886
references.finding: 17 LEO debris objects 1986-2024: decay rates rise sharply when SSN exceeds 67-75% of cycle peak; geomagnetic indices show minimal correlation with long-term decay (EUV dominates).

references.citation: The 2022 Starlink geomagnetic storms: Global thermospheric response to a high-latitude ionospheric driver. Space Weather (KNMI publication page; author list not verified)
references.finding: Moderate storms of 3-4 Feb 2022 raised thermospheric density (about 35-60% at 200-300 km); 38 of 49 Starlink satellites reentered in the following days.

references.citation: NBC News. How Orbital's falling satellite sparked a UFO mystery in South America
references.finding: Documented case of a satellite reentry generating UFO reports.

references.citation: Cockrell, R.C., Murphy, L., Rodeghier, M. Social factors and UFO reports: was the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic associated with an increase in UFO reporting? (SocArXiv doi:10.31235/osf.io/exm7c; Journal of Scientific Exploration)
references.finding: About 600 extra 2020 reports in each of NUFORC and MUFON; not explained by pandemic measures; correlated with Starlink launch timing, and removing Starlink-linked reports gave a 2020 decrease. Artificial-satellite activity is a major driver of report counts.

relationships.relationship: Geomagnetic activity x witness perception/behaviour (proposed mechanism by which space weather could modulate UAP reporting independent of any sky phenomenon)
relationships.summary: Persinger proposed that geophysical electromagnetic fields act on witnesses' temporal lobes and produce UFO-type experiences, e.g., 'Expected clinical consequences of close proximity to UFO-related luminosities' (1983). The core experimental support, weak complex magnetic fields evoking sensed presence, failed a double-blind replication (Granqvist et al. 2005, N = 89). Suggestibility traits, not the field, predicted outcomes. In the wider (non-UAP) literature on geomagnetic activity and human behaviour, results are mixed and often unreplicated. Pokorny & Mefferd (1966) found no influence of geomagnetic fluctuations on psychiatric admissions, suicides or homicides (Texas 1959-1961; 2,497 suicides, 2,017 homicides). Krivelyova & Robotti (2003, Atlanta Fed) reported lower equity returns in the 6 days after high-Ap periods (Ap > 29), attributed to mood misattribution. No study testing whether a perceptual/behavioural geomagnetic effect drives UAP report rates (as opposed to physical sky phenomena) was located.

references.citation: Persinger, M.A. (1983). Geophysical variables and behavior: IX. Expected clinical consequences of close proximity to UFO-related luminosities. Perceptual and Motor Skills 56:259-265
references.finding: Theoretical paper proposing physiological and neurobehavioural effects of geophysical luminosity fields on witnesses.

references.citation: Granqvist, P., Fredrikson, M., Unge, P., Hagenfeldt, A., Valind, S., Larhammar, D., Larsson, M. (2005). Sensed presence and mystical experiences are predicted by suggestibility, not by the application of transcranial weak complex magnetic fields. Neuroscience Letters 379(1):1-6
references.finding: Double-blind, sham-controlled (N = 89): no effect of weak complex magnetic fields; suggestibility predicted experiences. Undercuts Persinger's EM-perception mechanism.

references.citation: Pokorny, A.D., Mefferd, R.B. (1966). Geomagnetic fluctuations and disturbed behavior. Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 143(2):140-151
references.finding: Seven geomagnetic indices vs Texas suicides, homicides and psychiatric admissions 1959-1961: no influence found.

references.citation: Krivelyova, A., Robotti, C. (2003). Playing the field: Geomagnetic storms and the stock market. Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Working Paper 2003-5
references.finding: Reported lower equity returns after unusually high geomagnetic activity (Ap > 29), attributed to mood misattribution; an example of a claimed space-weather effect on aggregate human behaviour.

relationships.relationship: Solar-cycle autocorrelation as a confound / spurious-correlation generator in long time series of human-reported events (methodological precedent for any UAP x solar/geomagnetic test)
relationships.summary: Non-UAP literature shows repeatedly that the 11-year cycle, smoothing and nonstationarity produce spurious 'significant' correlations with human or societal series. Towers (2017) re-ran three published sunspot-influenza pandemic analyses and found no significant association, citing reproducibility and robustness failures. Boger, Hahn & Cumming (2000) showed that an apparent Homestake neutrino-sunspot anticorrelation appeared only with 3-, 5- and 7-point running averages and was an artifact of lost independence. Love et al. (2011) showed that secular sunspot/geomagnetic vs temperature correlations become non-significant once autocorrelation is handled (cycle averaging, first differencing). Granger & Newbold (1974) is the classic demonstration that regressions between independent integrated series give high R-squared and spurious significance. A 2026 EGUsphere preprint documents spurious correlations among space-weather indices themselves when the solar cycle is not filtered. Implication for UAP databases: report counts have strong secular trends (internet era, media waves, Starlink), and Kp/Ap/SSN share the cycle. Tests therefore need detrending or differencing, effective-degrees-of-freedom corrections, permutation or block-bootstrap nulls, and event-level designs rather than annual correlations.

references.citation: Towers, S. (2017). Sunspot activity and influenza pandemics: a statistical assessment of the purported association. Epidemiology and Infection
references.finding: Recreated three published analyses; in all cases no statistically significant sunspot-pandemic association; the faults found are common pitfalls (reproducibility, robustness).

references.citation: Boger, J., Hahn, R.L., Cumming, J.B. (2000). Do statistically significant correlations exist between the Homestake solar neutrino data and sunspots? arXiv:astro-ph/0001482
references.finding: Apparent anticorrelation appeared only with odd-length running averages and was an artifact of lost independence; no significant anticorrelation after proper subsampling.

references.citation: Love, J.J., Mursula, K., Tsai, V.C., Perkins, D.M. (2011). Are secular correlations between sunspots, geomagnetic activity, and global temperature significant? Geophysical Research Letters 38. doi:10.1029/2011GL049380
references.finding: Sunspot-geomagnetic correlation significant, but correlations of either with global temperature not significant after accounting for autocorrelation and nonstationarity.

references.citation: Granger, C.W.J., Newbold, P. (1974). Spurious regressions in econometrics. Journal of Econometrics 2(2):111-120. doi:10.1016/0304-4076(74)90034-7
references.finding: Regressions between independent random walks give spuriously significant coefficients, high R-squared and low Durbin-Watson statistics.

references.citation: Onah, C.I., Okike, O., Ugwoke, R.E., Iyida, E.U., Alhassan, J.A. (2026). Empirical evidence of spurious correlations among space weather variables. EGUsphere preprint egusphere-2025-6494 (under review)
references.finding: Correlations between space-weather indices and Forbush decreases changed or became inconsistent after filtering the 11-year cycle, so many apparent relations may be artifacts. Preprint with reviewer concerns.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x proximity to nuclear-weapons infrastructure (atomic labs, weapons storage, ICBM fields), spatial and historical
relationships.summary: This claim goes back to 1948-1952. USAF/ATIC (Ruppelt) noticed green-fireball and saucer reports bunching near Los Alamos, Sandia, Oak Ridge and Hanford, and treated them as a security concern. The 'rudimentary' 1950s USAF spatial analysis appears only in secondary accounts. No formal, population-adjusted Blue Book statistical study was found. Project Twinkle (1949-51) concluded the fireballs were probably natural. Robert Hastings (UFOs and Nukes, 2008) gathered testimony from more than 150 veterans about incidents at ICBM and weapons sites. This is anecdotal and has no denominator or control sites. Critics include James Carlson and Skeptical Inquirer. For Malmstrom Echo Flight (1967), the contemporaneous USAF/Boeing investigation found an electronic noise pulse and said UFO rumors were 'disproven'. A 2025 WSJ report, cited on Wikipedia, attributes it to a classified EMP test. The 1952 CIA study group's concern about objects near 'major US defense installations' is documented. NO DIRECT PRECEDENT LOCATED for a peer-reviewed, population/observer-adjusted test of US report rates near ICBM fields or weapons labs using NUFORC, Hatch, NICAP or Blue Book data. The only analyses found are anecdotal or descriptive, so the evidence is weak and confounded by observer density and heavy surveillance.

references.citation: Ruppelt, E.J. (1956). The Report on Unidentified Flying Objects, Chapter 4 (Wikisource)
references.finding: Green fireballs were concentrated within ~100 miles of Albuquerque, near Los Alamos and Sandia, 'one of the most sensitive security areas'. A qualitative concentration claim with no statistics.

references.citation: Hastings, R. (2008). UFOs and Nukes: Extraordinary Encounters at Nuclear Weapons Sites (publisher page)
references.finding: Testimony from 150+ ex-military personnel claiming a decades-long pattern of UFO activity at weapons labs, test sites, storage areas and ICBM launch facilities. Anecdotal, with no control comparison.

references.finding: Coverage of the Hastings/Salas press event making the nuclear-site claims.

references.finding: The 1967 USAF report says UFO rumors around Echo Flight were 'disproven'. Boeing/USAF tests found an electronic noise pulse, and a 2025 WSJ report attributes the shutdown to a classified EMP test.

references.finding: Critique of the Hastings/Salas Malmstrom claims: witness accounts are inconsistent and the crew commander reported no UFO.

references.finding: The 1952 CIA study group worried about objects 'in the vicinity of major US defense installations' and about the air-warning system being overloaded. Documents government concern, not a measured association.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x nuclear power plants / nuclear-risk industrial sites (civil nuclear infrastructure)
relationships.summary: Laurent, Thomas-Agnan & Vaillant (2015, arXiv) modeled GEIPAN reports from France (1951-2013) as an inhomogeneous spatial point pattern. Nuclear-risk sites remained a significant positive covariate (p = 0.00013) after controlling for population density. Contaminated land was also significant. The authors note this could reflect closer scrutiny of sensitive sites rather than a real excess of phenomena. It is a preprint, and no published replication was found. For the US, AARO's FY2024 report received 18 NNSA/NRC reports near nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, and all were categorized as UAS (drones). An anonymous, non-peer-reviewed Hugging Face analysis of about 105k geocoded NUFORC rows found no nuclear-specific lift: 57 nuclear plants vs 285 matched non-nuclear power plants within 50 miles gave a ratio of 0.85 and one-sided p = 0.85. NO DIRECT PRECEDENT LOCATED for a peer-reviewed, population-adjusted US test of civil nuclear plants.

references.citation: Laurent, T., Thomas-Agnan, C., Vaillant, M. (2015). Spatial Point Pattern Analysis of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in France. arXiv:1509.00571
references.finding: In GEIPAN data, intensity rose with population density, nuclear-risk sites (p=0.00013) and contaminated land. The authors offer surveillance or attention as an alternative explanation.

references.citation: AARO (Nov 2024). Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP (ODNI archive)
references.finding: 18 reports near US nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all categorized by NNSA/NRC as UAS. Ten flew over protected areas for under 5 minutes.

references.citation: Anonymous (n.d.). Nuclear-UAP public-source evidence surface (Hugging Face Space), non-peer-reviewed
references.finding: NUFORC reports within 50 mi: 57 nuclear plants vs 285 matched non-nuclear power plants, ratio 0.852 with one-sided p=0.85, so no nuclear-specific excess. Population and aviation proximity dominate.

references.citation: Wikipedia: UFO reports and atomic sites
references.finding: Summarizes the 2015 French result and the competing explanation that airspace around strategic sites is scrutinized more heavily.

relationships.relationship: UAP report counts (and POSS-I plate transients) x dates of atmospheric nuclear tests, 1949-1957 (temporal)
relationships.summary: Bruehl & Villarroel (2025, Scientific Reports 15:34125) used UFOCAT for daily UAP reports over 2,718 POSS-I observation days with 124 nuclear-test days. They report three associations. Transients were about 45% more likely within ±1 day of a test, peaking at +68% the day after. Each additional UFOCAT report was associated with about 8.5% more transients. The preprint also reports more UAP sightings inside test windows than outside them. All three are associations only. Watters et al. (2026, arXiv) found the test-transient correlation becomes insignificant once normalized for observation days, because it is driven by the Palomar observing schedule. They did not address the UAP reports. Doherty (2026, arXiv) reports an independent replication of the test-transient correlation. Hambly & Blair (2024) argue the transients are plate or emulsion artifacts. Other critics (Lupton, Kirkpatrick, cited in Scientific American) raise multiple-comparison problems and the possibility of balloons or debris near test sites. The direct link between UAP reports and nuclear-test dates rests on one group's analysis, has no independent replication, and is unresolved.

references.citation: Bruehl, S. & Villarroel, B. (2025). Transients in the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey (POSS-I) may be associated with nuclear testing and reports of unidentified anomalous phenomena. Scientific Reports 15, 34125. doi:10.1038/s41598-025-21620-3
references.finding: Transients were ~45% more likely within ±1 day of a nuclear test. Each extra UFOCAT UAP report was associated with ~8.5% more transients. The authors say this is not causal.

references.citation: Sci.News (2025). Mysterious Flashes in 1950s Skies Linked to Nuclear Tests and UAP Sightings: Study
references.finding: Gives the full citation and DOI. The UFOCAT data cover 2,428 of the study days, and the day-after-test peak is +68%.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x military operations areas (MOAs) / special-use airspace / training and testing ranges, spatial
relationships.summary: Government reports have repeatedly noted this. ODNI (2021) found UAP sightings 'tended to cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds' and attributed it to collection bias: focused attention, more sensors, unit expectations and guidance to report. ODNI (2022) said UAP events 'continue to occur in restricted or sensitive airspace' and gave the same collection-bias explanation. AARO FY2024 noted a 'continued geographic collection bias' near US military assets and sensors, with 81 reports from US military operating areas. For public reports, RAND (Posard, Gromis & Lee 2023) analyzed 101,151 NUFORC reports from 1998-2022 in 12,783 census places with a population offset. Being within 30 km of an MOA was the most consistent correlate: IRR 1.204 for all reports and 1.486 for reports inside spatial-scan clusters, against a 30-60 km reference. RAND interprets this as authorized military aircraft operating in MOAs. Limitations: the government reports concern military-sensor data, and the MOA layer is static, with no activation-time data, so it has not been tested against actual MOA usage. NO DIRECT PRECEDENT LOCATED for a test using MOA activation schedules.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x proximity to military installations/bases (distinct from MOAs)
relationships.summary: The two studies disagree, and neither shows a strong effect. Medina, Brewer & Kirkpatrick (2023, Sci Rep) analyzed 98,724 NUFORC reports from 2001-2020 with a county-level Bayesian Poisson model. The share of county area that is a military installation had a weak positive effect: RR 1.013 per SD, 95% CI 0.994-1.033, 92% posterior probability of being positive. RAND (2023) used census places with a population offset. Being within 30 km of Air Force, Army or Navy installations was associated with fewer reports than being 30-60 km away (IRR 0.837, 0.786 and 0.858). Marine Corps results went the other way, and RAND called the pattern inconsistent across distance and service branch. A 2018 blog analysis (Weird Data Science) of NUFORC density near USAF bases was visual only, with no formal test. The results depend on the spatial unit, the population adjustment and how 'installation' is defined.

references.finding: Military-installation area %: RR 1.013 (95% CI 0.994-1.033), only 92% posterior probability of being positive, so a weak association.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x airports / air-traffic density
relationships.summary: Published findings conflict in sign. Medina et al. (2023) used counties and airports per km² (all facility types). Air traffic had a positive effect: RR 1.099 per SD, 95% CI 1.068-1.131, with 100% posterior probability of being positive. RAND (2023) used census places with a population offset. Being within 60 km of a large or midsize civilian airport was associated with fewer reports per capita (IRR 0.831 and 0.821). RAND's reading is that people near airports are more familiar with aircraft. The difference is plausibly due to spatial unit, the population offset and the airport definition. Related evidence: a non-UAP FAA drone-sighting analysis (Bard 2015, 921 incidents) found most pilot-reported drone sightings within 5 miles of an airport, i.e. exposure scales with traffic. The FBI/DHS (Dec 2024) found many New Jersey 'drone' sightings were lawful manned aircraft. AARO FY2024 received 392 FAA reports, and only one involved a possible flight-safety issue.

references.finding: Airports per km² gave RR 1.099 (95% CI 1.068-1.131), a credible positive association with county NUFORC counts.

relationships.relationship: UAP light reports x military illumination / IR-countermeasure flare activity near ranges and warning areas
relationships.summary: Flares are well established as the cause in individual high-profile cases. The 10 pm Phoenix Lights (13 Mar 1997) were LUU-2B/B illumination flares dropped by Maryland ANG A-10s over the Barry M. Goldwater Range, about 60 miles away. The Guard confirmed this in July 1997, and a pilot confirmed it in 2007. LUU-2 flares burn about 5 minutes at roughly 1.8 million candlepower and descend about 8 ft/s, so from far away they look like a hovering row of lights. In a 2026-released case memo, AARO judged about 60% of a Western US 'orbs launching orbs' event plausibly attributable to IR countermeasure flares from a scheduled exercise; about 40% remained unresolved. Similar case-level attributions exist off the Carolinas coast (Pamlico Sound near BT-11/R-5306A, and Myrtle Beach reports linked to Shaw AFB flights), mostly from skeptic or press sources. NO DIRECT PRECEDENT LOCATED for a systematic time-series test linking report counts to range or warning-area activity or flare-exercise schedules. The relationship is well known case by case but has not been quantified.

relationships.relationship: UAP reports x military aerospace test activity: classified reconnaissance aircraft (U-2/OXCART) and missile/space launches (Plesetsk, Vandenberg twilight plumes)
relationships.summary: Haines' 1997 CIA history states that U-2 and OXCART test flights drove a large rise in pilot and controller UFO reports, and quotes the claim that 'over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s' were accounted for by manned reconnaissance flights. That fraction comes from a 1994 recollection with no supporting data, and critics (e.g., Peebles and Sheaffer, as summarized on Metabunk) consider it unsubstantiated. AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Vol. 1 concluded that most sightings were misidentified ordinary objects. It also found that interviewees had mistaken authentic classified programs for alien activity. Launch-produced optical phenomena are well established in the geophysics literature. Chernouss et al. (2012, Geophysica) document sunlit exhaust clouds from Plesetsk launches covering huge areas and generating 'UFO' media reports. The 1977 Petrozavodsk event was the Kosmos-955 launch. 'Space jellyfish' twilight plumes from Vandenberg and other launches are a known cause of reports. Existing work is mostly case-based. NO DIRECT PRECEDENT LOCATED for a population-adjusted time-series test of NUFORC or Hatch report spikes against launch catalogs, though the mechanism is well known.

relationships.relationship: UAP report counts (NUFORC/MUFON, national hotlines) x SpaceX Starlink launches and post-launch satellite trains
relationships.summary: There is a direct peer-reviewed precedent. Cockrell, Rodeghier & Murphy (J. Scientific Exploration, Feb 2023, DOI 10.31275/20222681) used NUFORC and MUFON data for 2018-2020. Reports rose by about 600 in each database in 2020 and did not track Google mobility or COVID-19 metrics. They did show a relationship between Starlink launches and later reports. With Starlink-linked reports removed, 2020 showed no statistical increase, and NUFORC actually fell. The same pattern appears outside the US: Belgium's hotline counted 210 reports in 2022 against 193 in 2021, with 22 reports from a single Starlink Falcon 9 launch on 21 Apr 2022. AARO's FY2025 report says Starlink is an increasingly common resolution, including one pilot report about an hour after a Cape Canaveral Starlink launch along the predicted orbital path. Limitations: the JSE venue is low-impact, there is no independent replication in a mainstream journal, and the launch-to-report lag and decay have not been published in detail. A non-peer-reviewed blog post titled 'Starlink Satellites do not Cause UFO Reports' disputes the effect, but its content could not be retrieved. Starlink launches therefore make a strong positive control, and the lag structure and per-launch effect size are still open to quantify.

references.finding: About 600 extra reports in each database in 2020. Starlink launches were followed by reports. With Starlink-linked reports removed there was no 2020 increase (NUFORC decreased). No association with pandemic mobility or health factors.

relationships.relationship: Pilot/aviation UAP reports x satellite (Starlink) specular flaring geometry (sun depression angle, near-horizon, solar azimuth, recently launched trains)
relationships.summary: Several reconstructions tie this down. Buettner, Griffiths, Snell & Stilley (arXiv 2403.08155, 2024; IAA SSA conference) reconstructed a 10 Aug 2022 event using TLE, ADS-B and visualization: five pilots on two airliners over the Pacific. The 'UAP' was the Starlink 4-26 train launched that day, crossing the terminator about 1620 km from AC536. Mallama & Cole (arXiv 2405.13091, 2024) showed 'extreme flaring' at magnitude -5 to -6 (Venus-like). This happens when sunlight strikes the flat chassis or arrays at grazing incidence, with the train near the horizon close to the solar azimuth and the Sun about 30 deg below the horizon. AARO released 'Correlations of Starlink Satellite Flaring with UAP Observations' (Jan 2025). Its FY2025 report attributes 238 cases to satellite flaring through 3D modelling, including all 44 space-domain events (42 FAA pilot reports and 2 SPACECOM reports). A testable prediction is that pilot reports cluster at specific solar-depression and look angles. No published population-level test against the full FAA/NUFORC record was located. No quantitative study linking ISS pass times to NUFORC reports was located either; ISS and other bright satellites are documented only as anecdotal IFO sources (Hendry 1979: satellites about 2% of 1,307 cases).

references.citation: Buettner D.J., Griffiths R.E., Snell N., Stilley J. (2024). Enhancing Space Situational Awareness to Mitigate Risk: A Case Study in the Misidentification of Starlink Satellites as UAP in Commercial Aviation. arXiv:2403.08155
references.finding: The 10 Aug 2022 multi-pilot UAP was the same-day Starlink 4-26 train under unusual illumination. The authors call for pilot advisories and data sharing.

relationships.relationship: UAP report clusters x twilight rocket/missile launches (illuminated exhaust plumes, 'space jellyfish', upper-stage fuel dumps; Vandenberg, Cape Canaveral, Plesetsk, White Sea)
relationships.summary: This is well documented at the level of individual events. A launch shortly after sunset or before sunrise puts high-altitude exhaust in sunlight while observers are in darkness, producing a glowing expanding 'jellyfish' that triggers waves of UFO and missile-strike reports. Documented cases: Petrozavodsk 1977 (Kosmos-955 from Plesetsk; Oberg); the Norway spiral of 9 Dec 2009 (failed Bulava SLBM, hundreds of calls); Vandenberg Iridium launch of 22 Dec 2017 (calls across S. California and Arizona, LAFD advisory); 2013 Falcon 9 upper-stage fuel venting seen from southern Africa and Mauritius about 1 h after launch; and many later Vandenberg Starlink twilight launches (one prompted 7 AMS fireball reports). AARO FY2025 resolved one case to a commercial rocket launch. The Nov 1957 US wave (Levelland and others) began the night Sputnik 2 was launched. Blue Book-era commentators attributed it partly to people sky-watching for the satellite, which is an attention effect rather than misidentification of the vehicle itself. No peer-reviewed systematic time-series test was located that links NUFORC daily or regional counts to launch time, solar depression angle and plume geometry. That quantification, and its use as a positive control, appears open.

relationships.relationship: UAP report rates x visibility/brightness of Venus and bright planets (greatest elongation, conjunctions; historical Mars-opposition periodicity claim)
relationships.summary: Stars and planets as a category of identified objects (IFOs) are well established. Hendry (1979, CUFOS, 1,307 cases) found bright stars and planets made up 29% of all reports, the largest night-time category. Blue Book Special Report 14 (3,201 cases, 1951-54) put astronomical explanations at 22% of IFOs. Venus is the classic stimulus, including police 'chases'; the Portage County 1966 Venus attribution was disputed by Hynek. Whether report rates rise in time with Venus's elongation or brightness cycle has only been suggested, not tested at scale. Holman (2013) argued that Venus at maximum elongation (11 Feb 1913) drove the 1913 British 'scareship' wave, using an admittedly non-rigorous directional tabulation: west was the most common final bearing. A NUFORC posting (Mar 2023) notes a heavy spike in reports during the late-Feb/early-Mar 2023 Venus-Jupiter conjunction. As a cautionary precedent, Vallée & Vallée (1960s) reported that UFO waves tracked Mars oppositions (about 26-month cycle, p<0.001 after an ad hoc 2-month shift). The pattern failed in 1947 and 1957 and is generally regarded as spurious. No peer-reviewed time-series analysis of NUFORC or GEIPAN counts against Venus elongation/magnitude, controlling for season and twilight duration, was located.

relationships.relationship: UAP report rates x meteors, fireballs/bolides and annual meteor showers
relationships.summary: Meteors and fireballs are a standard IFO category: Hendry found meteors and space debris made up about 9% of 1,307 cases, and Blue Book attributed individual case clusters to showers (e.g., the Perseids, 12 Aug 1951). The only quantitative NUFORC-vs-shower analysis located is Lund (arXiv 2303.17103, 2023). It is an explicitly satirical April-Fools paper ('Acta Prima Aprilia'). It reports that the median daily NUFORC count on shower days (255.5) is 29% above the all-day median (198). It does not control for season: the Perseids fall in the July/August reporting peak. So a properly deseasonalized test of shower peaks, or of individual AMS-reported fireballs, against UAP reports has no serious published precedent. Perception literature supports the mechanism. Rospars (2023) assessed about 300 French police-recorded witness accounts of 7 meteoroid and satellite atmospheric entries (1980-2009). Reliability was near zero for distance, height and direction of motion, and 0.5 to almost 1 for directly perceptible attributes. Non-UAP fireball science (AMS reporting statistics) offers matched covariates.

references.finding: Over 80,000 NUFORC reports. Median reports on meteor-shower days are 29% higher than the all-day median. The paper is satirical and does not control for season.
