relationships.relationship: Multi-witness 'structured craft' UAP reports x satellite/rocket-stage atmospheric re-entries
relationships.summary: Re-entries are classic stimuli for widespread, coherent reports of a structured craft. On 5 Nov 1990 (about 19:00) the re-entry of the Proton upper stage from the Gorizont-21 launch (1990-094C) crossed France from Pau to Strasbourg. It produced about 100 written and as many phoned testimonies in Alsace alone, plus police and gendarmerie reports, many describing a triangle or diamond of lights. SEPRA (now GEIPAN) confirmed the re-entry with NASA data. The Condon Report (1968) analysed the 3 Mar 1968 Zond-4-related re-entry, where witnesses described a rocket ship with windows; Hartmann compared it to Chiles-Whitted 1947. CNES/GEIPAN lists re-entries of satellites and rocket stages among its standard identifications. Rospars' reliability study used such entries as ground truth. A systematic test linking catalogued re-entries (e.g., Aerospace/Space-Track decay predictions) to clusters in NUFORC or GEIPAN was not located beyond case studies.

references.citation: SeeSat-L archive (Dec 2005). Request info on Gorizont/Proton re-entry on Nov. 5, 1990
references.finding: Identifies the 5 Nov 1990 object as the Gorizont-21 Proton stage (1990-094C / 20925).

references.citation: Patrick Gross press archive. Sud-Ouest, 8 Nov 1990 (French press coverage of the 5 Nov 1990 re-entry)
references.finding: Widespread French reports of a triangle or diamond of lights. SEPRA verified a re-entry using NASA data.

references.citation: The Black Vault. The full Condon Committee report on UFOs (1968)
references.finding: Includes Hartmann's analysis of the Zond IV re-entry, which witnesses perceived as a structured craft with windows.

references.citation: CNES. Les OVNIS (ou PAN) - GEIPAN overview
references.finding: Over 60% of cases get rational explanations. Re-entries of satellites and rocket stages, bolides and celestial bodies are listed as standard causes. About 700 reports a year.

references.citation: Rospars J.-P. (2023). Eyewitness abilities and limitations on atmospheric entries
references.finding: Using re-entries as ground truth, witness distance and height estimates are essentially unreliable.

relationships.relationship: Orange-light/orb UAP reports and national report surges x sky (Chinese/Thai) lantern releases (weddings, parties, public holidays; ~2006-2014 fad)
relationships.summary: Lanterns are documented by two governments. GEIPAN issued a public notice calling flying lanterns 'une méprise courante': about 400,000 are sold each year in France, and since about 2008 it has received many reports of silent orange spheres that investigations quickly attributed to lanterns. Investigators routinely check town halls for weddings or celebrations. In the UK, MoD files released by The National Archives show reports trebling in 2009 (over 600) and attribute the surge partly to 'the craze for releasing Chinese lanterns at weddings and public holidays'; Dr David Clarke notes the formations of slowly moving orange lights. A 2025 analysis of about 2,492 MoD reports (1997-2009) describes a 2007-2009 phase dominated by 'orange/red lights/orbs/fireballs'; it is a web article and not peer-reviewed. An exact share of lanterns among GEIPAN identifications could not be verified from a primary source, because GEIPAN pages were rate-limited (HTTP 429). One unverifiable search snippet claimed 20.5% overall and a 44% peak in 2014. That should be computed from the GEIPAN case files rather than cited. Lanterns should yield season, weekend and holiday signatures (14 July, New Year, Bonfire Night) and colour/shape keywords.

references.citation: GEIPAN/CNES. Information GEIPAN - Les lanternes volantes: une méprise courante (public notice PDF)
references.finding: About 400,000 Thai lanterns are sold a year in France. Since about 2008 there have been many reports of silent orange spheres, which investigations identified as lanterns.

references.citation: The National Archives (UK). Final tranche of UFO files released (press release on DEFE 24 files, 2007-2009)
references.finding: Over 600 reports in 2009, treble the previous year. The surge is partly attributed to Chinese lanterns at weddings and public holidays, and partly to increased publicity.

references.citation: New Space Economy (12 Nov 2025). A comprehensive analysis of UK unidentified aerial phenomena reports 1997-2009
references.finding: About 2,492 MoD reports. 2008 = 285 and 2009 = 384 logged. 2007-2009 descriptions are dominated by orange/red lights and orbs, coinciding with the popularity of lanterns. Not peer-reviewed.

references.citation: Mellow C. (Sept 2010). Department of Flying Saucers. Air & Space/Smithsonian
references.finding: GEIPAN-solved cases include mysterious lights over Brittany that were Chinese lanterns. About 23% of cases were then unidentified.

relationships.relationship: NUFORC daily report spikes x fireworks holidays (US Independence Day, New Year's Eve/Day)
relationships.summary: Widely reported, but documented only in non-peer-reviewed analyses of NUFORC data. Costa (Syracuse New Times) finds 4 July is the single top date: 2.11% of about 121,000 sightings in 2001-2015. Popular Science reports 2,863 sightings on Independence Day in 2001-2018, more than seven times the 24-hour average. A NUFORC technical director attributes this to misidentified fireworks plus more people outdoors. A blog analysis estimates that days near 4 July and New Year's Eve together account for only about 4% of sightings, so the effect is large per day but small in aggregate. Costa also notes unexplained peaks on the 15th of several months. These are most likely reporter date-rounding artifacts and should be handled as data-quality confounds in any day-level test. No peer-reviewed estimate that separates the fireworks stimulus from the outdoor-exposure effect was located, for example by comparing shape or colour keywords or holidays without fireworks.

references.citation: Costa C. New York Skies: The top day for UFO sightings. Syracuse New Times
references.finding: 4 July = 2.11% of about 121,000 NUFORC sightings (2001-2015), the top date. New Year's is also elevated. Puzzling peaks fall on the 15th of the month.

references.citation: Popular Science. UFO sightings say more about us than about aliens (charted NUFORC data)
references.finding: 2,863 sightings on 4 July in 2001-2018, more than 7 times the daily average. About three-quarters of timestamped reports fall at 5-11 pm.

references.citation: Fox News. What is the best day to spot a UFO (NUFORC technical director quoted)
references.finding: NUFORC staff attribute the 4 July peak to misidentified fireworks.

references.citation: Hradek N. (Medium blog). How Many UFO Reports Can Be Attributed to the 4th of July? (seen in search; fetch returned 403)
references.finding: Per search snippet: about 4% of sightings coincide with days near 4 July and New Year's Eve combined.

relationships.relationship: UAP report density/rates x background density of conventional aerial objects (air traffic, military areas, balloons, drones) and sky-view opportunity
relationships.summary: Medina, Brewer & Kirkpatrick (Scientific Reports 2023) fitted a Bayesian spatial Poisson model to 98,724 NUFORC reports in the contiguous US (2001-2020). Air traffic per km2 gave rate ratio 1.099 per SD (credibility 100%) and military area 1.013 (92%). Light pollution gave 0.923 (fewer reports), tree canopy 0.961, and cloud cover had no credible effect. The authors interpret this as people seeing real but unrecognized objects when they have more chance to look. Government case resolutions agree. ODNI's 2022 report covered 366 reports: 163 balloon or balloon-like, 26 UAS, 6 clutter, 171 uncharacterized. AARO FY2024 resolved hundreds of cases to balloons, birds, UAS, satellites and aircraft; secondary summaries put balloons at about 70%, but that was not verified in the PDF (403). AARO FY2025 closed 114 incoming cases, 60 of them balloons. The NASA UAP Independent Study Team (Sept 2023) explicitly recommends a 'background signals' database. It would cover launch rates of weather, scientific, commercial, hobbyist and military balloons, aircraft counts and daily drone launch rates, plus systematic metadata and crowd-sourced calibrated reporting. That database has not yet been built publicly. The spatial result exists, but time-resolved tests that use actual balloon-launch or ADS-B traffic counts as covariates appear open.

references.citation: Medina R.M., Brewer S.C., Kirkpatrick S.M. (2023). An environmental analysis of public UAP sightings and sky view potential. Scientific Reports 13
references.finding: 98,724 NUFORC reports. Air traffic RR 1.099/SD, military 1.013, light pollution 0.923, canopy 0.961, cloud cover null.

references.citation: NASA UAP Independent Study Team (Sept 2023). Final Report
references.finding: Recommends characterizing the background (balloon launch rates, aircraft counts, daily drone launches, appearance and motion signatures), metadata and calibration standards, and crowd-sourced smartphone reporting. Found no evidence of extraterrestrial origin.

references.citation: NPR (13 Jan 2023). The Pentagon got hundreds of new reports of UFOs in 2022 (ODNI 2022 Annual Report on UAP)
references.finding: 366 reports: 163 balloon or balloon-like, 26 UAS, 6 clutter, 171 uncharacterized.

references.citation: DefenseScoop (14 Nov 2024). AARO chief unveils Pentagon annual caseload analysis (FY2024 Consolidated Annual Report)
references.finding: 757 new reports (May 2023 to Jun 2024). Hundreds resolved to balloons, birds, drones, satellites and aircraft, including Starlink flares. Over 900 lack sufficient data.

references.citation: DoD/AARO (Nov 2024). FY2024 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP (PDF; seen in search results, fetch returned 403)
references.finding: Primary source for the FY2024 resolution categories. Per secondary summaries, balloons were the largest share of resolved cases.

relationships.relationship: Daytime disc/saucer UAP reports x lenticular (mountain-wave) cloud occurrence
relationships.summary: The precedent here is anecdotal only. Popular and meteorological sources say altocumulus lenticularis is often mistaken for UFOs, and one claims an Air Force investigation explained Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting this way; that claim was not verified against a primary source. No study was located that quantitatively links UAP reports to lenticular or mountain-wave conditions, such as lee-wave forecasts, METAR or synoptic cloud-type codes, or terrain-wind indices. The closest null result is Medina et al. (2023): total cloud cover had no credible association with NUFORC county rates. That speaks to cloud amount, not lenticular type. Non-UAP meteorology gives the needed covariates. NWS and MeteoSwiss explain the mountain-wave mechanism. A 50-year Katowice synoptic climatology (1971-2020) shows Ac lenticularis peaks in Oct-Nov, is least frequent in April, and declines by 2.7 days per decade. This relationship appears untested.

references.citation: Popular Science. These saucer-shaped clouds look just like UFOs
references.finding: Anecdotal: lenticular clouds are frequently reported as UFOs. No quantitative data.

references.citation: RCIN repository. Climatology of altocumulus lenticularis in Katowice, 1971-2020
references.finding: Ac len is most frequent in Oct-Nov and least in April, with a significant decline of -2.7 days per decade. This is a non-UAP covariate source.

references.citation: NWS Honolulu. Lenticular clouds
references.finding: Explains how mountain waves form lenticular clouds.

references.citation: Medina R.M. et al. (2023). Scientific Reports
references.finding: Cloud cover RR 0.998 (52% credibility): no credible association with NUFORC report rates.

relationships.relationship: UAP report counts x media / pop-culture events, official disclosures (1996 X-Files/Independence Day, Dec-2017 NYT AATIP story, 2021 ODNI report) and social attention/stigma
relationships.summary: The idea that report waves follow media and official disclosure has been around for a long time, but almost all of the support is descriptive or asserted rather than causally estimated. David Clarke's summary of UK MoD files reported a jump from 117 sightings (1995) to 609 (1996). He linked it to The X-Files and Independence Day, and noted that 1978, the year Close Encounters came out, was another peak year. This is a coincidence of annual counts with no control series. ODNI's 2022 report says the rise in US government UAP reporting (247 new reports plus 119 others, 510 in total by Aug 2022) is 'partially due to reduced stigma'. NASA's 2023 independent study team says stigma 'almost certainly leads to data attrition'. Both are expert judgements, not tests. RAND's NUFORC series (by observation year, 1998-2022) shows counts rising to 2014, falling 2015-2018 and rising again 2019-2020. That pattern does not suggest a large lasting jump after the Dec-2017 NYT story. Cockrell, Murphy & Rodeghier (JSE 2023) found a significant 2020 rise in NUFORC/MUFON reports, but it had little or no association with pandemic measures. The rise disappeared once Starlink reports were removed, so a misidentification source, not a social mechanism, explained that wave. Goldstein & Raveh (SSRN 2023) treat UAP reports as a measure of public attention. They find more reports in wealthier regions and a counter-cyclical pattern within regions, using COVID restrictions as a natural experiment. Warren (Science 1970) proposed a social-status explanation for who reports sightings. No formal event-study or interrupted-time-series analysis of civilian databases around the 2017 NYT or 2021 ODNI releases was located, so a matched-window event study would add something. A null result there would agree with RAND's trend and the Starlink finding.

references.citation: Universe Today (summarizing David Clarke's analysis of UK Ministry of Defence UFO files 1981-1996), 'Report: UFO Sightings Coincide with Popular Sci-Fi Films, TV'
references.finding: UK MoD sightings went from 117 (1995) to 609 (1996), which coincided with The X-Files and Independence Day. Clarke attributes the rise to heightened awareness leading to more reports. About 90% of cases had mundane explanations.

references.citation: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (2023 release, data to Aug 2022), 2022 Annual Report on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
references.finding: Assesses that the increased UAP reporting rate is partly due to more awareness of UAP as flight hazards or adversary collection platforms, and partly due to reduced stigma. 510 reports catalogued by 30 Aug 2022.

references.citation: NASA UAP Independent Study Team (2023), Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Independent Study Team Report
references.finding: States that stigma around UAP reporting 'almost certainly leads to data attrition'. Recommends destigmatization and calibrated, metadata-rich data collection.

references.citation: Posard M.N., Gromis A., Lee M. (2023), Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America, RAND RR-A2475-1
references.finding: 101,151 NUFORC sightings, 1998-2022. Counts rose to 2014 (sharply 2012-2014), fell 2015-2018, rose 2019-2020, then returned to about 2018 levels in 2021. Average 1.76 reports per 100,000 people per year.

references.citation: Cockrell R.C., Murphy L., Rodeghier M. (2023), Social Factors and UFO Reports: Was the SARS-CoV-2 Pandemic Associated with an Increase in UFO Reporting?, Journal of Scientific Exploration 36(4)
references.finding: 2020 reports were up on 2019 (p<0.001) but had little or no association with mobility or COVID case/death measures. The excess vanished after Starlink reports were filtered out.

references.citation: Goldstein N., Raveh O. (2023), Looking Up The Sky: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena and Macroeconomic Attention, SSRN 4424455
references.finding: Treats UAP reports as a measure of attention. More reports in wealthier regions, with a counter-cyclical pattern within regions. COVID restrictions used as a natural experiment, and the metric correlates with standard attention measures.

relationships.relationship: UAP report hour-of-day distribution ('law of the times') x sky darkness and witness availability
relationships.summary: This is a well-established pattern. Poher & Vallee (AIAA paper 75-42, 1975) described it for close-encounter (type-I) reports. Reports are low in daytime, rise from about 17h, peak near 21h, dip at about 01h, show a secondary peak near 03h and are back to baseline by 06h. They read the shape as a witness-availability effect and estimated that witnesses see about 1 in 14 close approaches. Ballester Olmos' FOTOCAT analysis (about 4,800 timed cases, 1947-2005) found that UFO and IFO (identified) hour-of-day curves are almost identical (r=0.94, 1947-1999). He states the law of the times 'emerges in the same manner in both unexplained and explained sets'. Across catalogs, correlations reach 0.96 (Vallee vs Hatch). Hatch's catalog forms a near-Gaussian curve centered on 22h with no secondary peak. Plaza del Olmo modelled the curve from sun altitude and visual limiting magnitude plus population social habits, and reports these factors alone reproduce the 21-22h peak (author page, not peer-reviewed). Popular NUFORC analyses (The Economist, discussed by Novella 2014) show the same evening peak, explained by darkness plus people being awake. A day-of-week analysis in peer-reviewed literature was not located, and Poher & Vallee do not address it. A replication on NUFORC/GEIPAN/Hatch is therefore a positive control, not a discovery.

references.citation: Poher C., Vallee J. (1975), Basic Patterns in UFO Observations, AIAA 13th Aerospace Sciences Meeting, Paper 75-42
references.finding: Type-I reports peak at about 21h, with a secondary peak at about 03h. The authors attribute the shape to observer availability and estimate witnesses are positioned to see about 1 in 14 close approaches.

references.citation: Ballester Olmos V.J. (c. 2013), UFO Reports by Time of the Day, FOTOCAT report
references.finding: UFO and IFO hourly curves correlate at r=0.94 (1947-1999), and the law of the times appears equally in explained and unexplained sets. Inter-catalog correlations are 0.46-0.99. The Hatch catalog is Gaussian, centered at 22h.

references.citation: Plaza del Olmo J., papers on the Law of Times (academia.edu author page)
references.finding: Models the law of the times from sun altitude and visual limiting magnitude (visibility) times a social-availability factor. These alone reproduce the 21-22h main peak.

references.citation: Novella S. (2014), Distribution of UFO Sightings, NeuroLogica blog (discussing The Economist's NUFORC graphic)
references.finding: NUFORC reports peak in evening hours. Novella explains this as night being better for seeing unidentified lights while people are still awake, rather than alcohol.

relationships.relationship: Apparent astronomical periodicity (local sidereal time) in UAP catalogs x duplicate / non-independent records
relationships.summary: Sturrock (JSE 2004) reported a local-sidereal-time (LST) modulation in about 12,200 events from Larry Hatch's *U* catalog. Earlier LST claims came from Poher (1973) and from Johnson (UFOCAT CE2/CE3, p<1e-7). Vallee re-analysed 11,991 Hatch events (1947-2000) and reproduced Sturrock's LST distribution. A control with a French catalogue then showed that multiple entries for a single notable event had produced massively duplicated records, which casts doubt on the LST pattern. Ballester Olmos concludes that patterns, or their absence, 'reflect the internal quality and size of the samples'. This is a direct precedent for deduplicating and clustering events before temporal or astronomical tests. Any periodicity found in raw records but not in deduplicated clusters should be treated as an artefact.

references.citation: Vallee J.F. (c. 2005), Are UFO Events related to Sidereal Time? Arguments against a proposed correlation
references.finding: Reproduced Sturrock's LST peak in 11,991 Hatch events. A control with a French catalogue showed that duplicated records of single events create the pattern.

references.citation: Sturrock P.A. (2004), Time-Series Analysis of a Catalog of UFO Events: Evidence of a Local-Sidereal-Time Modulation, Journal of Scientific Exploration 18(3):405 (URL as cited by Ballester Olmos; now redirects to the JSE site)
references.finding: Reported that the event rate in the Hatch catalog depends on local sidereal time.

references.citation: Ballester Olmos V.J. (c. 2013), UFO Reports by Time of the Day, FOTOCAT report
references.finding: Notes that sidereal-time correlations remain unsettled, and that apparent patterns depend on catalog quality, size and redundancy.

relationships.relationship: Area-level observation opportunity (light pollution, tree canopy, cloud climatology, population, airports, military airspace) x UAP report rates
relationships.summary: Several recent analyses of NUFORC cover this directly. Medina, Brewer & Kirkpatrick (Sci Rep 2023) studied 98,724 reports (2001-2020) by county using Bayesian spatial Poisson (INLA) models. Per SD increase: light pollution -7.7% and tree canopy -3.9% in per-capita reports, airports per km2 +9.9%, military installations +1.3%. Cloud-cover climatology had no credible effect. Their reading is that people see more 'phenomena' when they have more opportunity to look. RAND (2023; 101,151 reports in 12,783 census places, 1998-2022) found its most consistent effect within 30 km of military operations areas (MOAs). It found negative associations near civilian airports, near radiosonde weather stations and in denser areas, and suggests better-informed populations report less. A 2026 SocArXiv preprint (about 59,000 reports, about 3,000 counties, 1995-2014) found population size dominant, consistent with reporting opportunity. It also reported aviation, geomagnetic, elevation, seismic, nuclear, petroleum and Air Force covariates, with 82% of county variance explained (not peer-reviewed). Outside UAP work, Kyba et al. (Science 2023) document a rapid global loss of naked-eye star visibility from 2011 to 2022, which supports light pollution as a time-varying observation covariate. Area-level replication is a positive control. Signs differ between studies (e.g., population density per capita), so results depend on the denominator and spatial unit.

references.citation: Medina R.M., Brewer S.C., Kirkpatrick S.M. (2023), An environmental analysis of public UAP sightings and sky view potential, Scientific Reports 13
references.finding: Per SD: light pollution -7.7%, tree canopy -3.9%, airports +9.9%, military installations +1.3%, cloud cover not credible. County Poisson INLA model, 98,724 NUFORC reports.

references.citation: Posard M.N., Gromis A., Lee M. (2023), Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America, RAND RR-A2475-1
references.finding: Most consistent effect: reports within 30 km of MOAs. Negative associations within 60 km of civilian airports, within 30 km of weather stations and in denser areas. Effects of distance to military installations are inconsistent.

references.citation: (2026) Geospatial Predictors of Unidentified Aerial Phenomenon Reports Across U.S. Counties, SocArXiv preprint
references.finding: Population size is the dominant predictor (reporting opportunity). Aviation infrastructure, geomagnetic anomalies, elevation, seismicity, nuclear/petroleum facilities and AF bases are also significant. R2 about 0.82 at county level.

references.citation: Alshehri L.A. (2025), Spatial Analysis of the Distribution of UAP Sightings: An Analytical Study of Natural and Human Factors, Beni-Suef University Int. J. Humanities and Social Sciences 7(2)
references.finding: Spatial analysis of natural and human factors in UAP sighting distribution. Only the title and metadata were seen; the abstract was not available.

references.citation: Kyba C.C.M. et al. (2023), Citizen scientists report global rapid reductions in the visibility of stars from 2011 to 2022, Science
references.finding: Documents a rapid loss of naked-eye star visibility from growing skyglow. Non-UAP evidence that the sky-viewing opportunity covariate changes over time.

relationships.relationship: Day-level sky-viewing conditions (daily cloud cover, moonlight / lunar sky brightness) x within-location probability of a UAP report
relationships.summary: No study was located that estimates the effect of day-specific cloud cover or Moon phase/altitude on UAP reporting within a location, for example with self-matched controls. The closest UAP work is Medina et al. (2023), whose cloud variable is county climatology (no credible effect). Another is the hour-of-day models (Poher & Vallee 1975; Plaza del Olmo), which use sun altitude and limiting magnitude as visibility factors. Outside UAP work, the physics is established. Krisciunas & Schaefer (PASP 1991) give the standard model of sky brightness from moonlight, which lowers the limiting magnitude and so should reduce how visible faint lights are. Searches for UFO reports and lunar phase found nothing relevant. A within-location daily design (e.g., a time-stratified case-crossover) testing cloud and moonlight effects therefore appears new for UAP data. Expected signs are fewer reports under overcast skies and bright moonlit skies, except reports that are themselves Moon misidentifications.

references.citation: Medina R.M., Brewer S.C., Kirkpatrick S.M. (2023), An environmental analysis of public UAP sightings and sky view potential, Scientific Reports 13
references.finding: Cloud cover entered only as an area-level climatological covariate and had no credible relationship. No daily or within-location weather analysis.

references.citation: Krisciunas K., Schaefer B.E. (1991), A model of the brightness of moonlight, Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific
references.finding: Standard model of night-sky brightening by moonlight as a function of lunar phase, altitude and separation. Gives the physical basis for moonlight reducing how visible faint lights are.

references.citation: Poher C., Vallee J. (1975), Basic Patterns in UFO Observations, AIAA Paper 75-42
references.finding: Visibility and observer availability explain the hour-of-day pattern. The paper does not treat daily weather or the Moon.

references.citation: Plaza del Olmo J., papers on the Law of Times (academia.edu author page)
references.finding: Uses sun altitude and visual limiting magnitude as visibility terms in an hour-of-day model. No daily cloud or moonlight analysis was seen.

relationships.relationship: Case quality / credibility and strangeness ratings x probability that a case remains unexplained (Battelle, Hynek S-P, GEIPAN D class, Hatch, Vallee SVP)
relationships.summary: Battelle Memorial Institute's Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 (1955) found that better-quality reports were more often 'unknown': 35% of 'excellent' cases versus 18% of the poorest. Hynek's The UFO Experience (1972, reviewed in Science) introduced the close-encounter typology and rating reports by strangeness and probability (credibility). GEIPAN reserves class D for phenomena that stay unexplained despite precise testimony and good-quality material evidence. That makes D partly a quality-conditioned label; about 3% of about 1,600 cases are D. Ballester Olmos shows UFO and IFO cases share the same hour-of-day profile (r=0.94), so 'unexplained' status is not separable from reporting conditions on that variable. ODNI 2021 stresses 'the limited amount of high-quality reporting': 144 USG reports, 80 involving multiple sensors. A caution from this literature: if quality criteria feed into the 'unknown' or D label, the quality-unknown association is partly circular. That is an argument for scoring quality without narrative strangeness, as this study does. A primary source for Vallee's SVP rating could not be verified online, and documentation of Hatch credibility/strangeness fields beyond Vallee's description of a 'consistent coding system' was not located.

references.citation: Wikipedia, Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 (Battelle Memorial Institute, 1955)
references.finding: 35% of 'excellent' quality cases were unknowns versus 18% of the poorest-quality cases.

references.citation: Murray B.C. (1972), review of J.A. Hynek, The UFO Experience: A Scientific Inquiry, Science 177:688
references.finding: Review of Hynek's book, which set out the close-encounter classification and the strangeness/probability rating of reports.

references.citation: Hynek J.A. (1973), An Unemotional Analysis: The UFO Experience, The Physics Teacher
references.finding: Hynek's own summary for physicists of his approach to classifying and evaluating UFO reports.

references.citation: Wikipedia (fr), Groupe d'etudes et d'informations sur les phenomenes aerospatiaux non identifies (GEIPAN)
references.finding: Class D is defined as unexplainable despite precise testimony and good-quality material evidence. About 3% of about 1,600 cases.

references.citation: ODNI (2021), Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
references.finding: Limited high-quality data and inconsistent reporting. 144 USG reports, 80 multi-sensor. No standardized mechanism until March 2019. Stigma and reputational risk keep observers silent.

references.citation: Ballester Olmos V.J. (c. 2013), UFO Reports by Time of the Day, FOTOCAT report
references.finding: Explained (IFO) and unexplained (UFO) cases have the same hourly distribution (r=0.94).

relationships.relationship: Kulldorff spatial scan clusters of UAP reports (and their association with military airspace)
relationships.summary: RAND (2023) has already applied Kulldorff's spatial scan statistic to NUFORC. They used a discrete Poisson model with census-place population as exposure, a maximum radius of 60 km (about the visual horizon), separate runs per year from 1998 to 2022, and 999 Monte Carlo replications. They then related cluster membership and counts to military installations, MOAs, weather stations and airports. Proximity to an MOA (within 30 km) was the most consistent predictor. Results were robust to 50/100 km radii and to excluding Washington/Oregon, which held persistent clusters. Earlier spatial-pattern claims in flap data, such as Aime Michel's 1954 'orthoteny' (BaVic line), were later questioned on statistical grounds (Saunders, FSR 1971). These show why Monte Carlo significance against a population baseline is needed. Running a Kulldorff scan on NUFORC is not new. What may be new is scanning high-quality or unexplained subsets against an explained-report baseline, or replicating across sources.

references.citation: Posard M.N., Gromis A., Lee M. (2023), Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America, RAND RR-A2475-1
references.finding: Kulldorff spatial scan (60 km maximum radius, yearly, 999 Monte Carlo) on 101,151 NUFORC reports. Significant clusters, with the most consistent association being within 30 km of MOAs.

references.citation: Kulldorff M. (1997), A spatial scan statistic, Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods
references.finding: Original spatial scan statistic with Monte Carlo inference, adjusted for multiple cluster locations and sizes.

references.citation: Wikipedia, Orthoteny
references.finding: Aime Michel's claim that 1954 French flap sightings fell on straight lines (BaVic). Saunders' 'Is Bavic Remarkable?' tested it statistically. An early example of a spatial-pattern claim from flap data.

relationships.relationship: Time-stratified case-crossover design, Knox space-time interaction test, two-way cluster-robust variance and negative-control empirical p-value calibration applied to UAP report data
relationships.summary: All four methods are standard in epidemiology and econometrics. They are Maclure's (1991) case-crossover design and Janes, Sheppard & Lumley's (2005) time-stratified referent selection, which avoids overlap bias; Knox's (1964) space-time interaction test; Cameron, Gelbach & Miller's (2011) multiway cluster-robust variance; and Schuemie et al.'s (2014) empirical calibration of p-values using negative controls. No application of any of them to UAP or UFO report data was located in UAP-specific bibliographic searches (Crossref, Europe PMC, web). The closest UAP analog is Coleman (JSE 2023), a data-driven screen of NUFORC sightings against 19 global parameters at annual or monthly resolution. Its abstract reports 'diverse' associations and mentions no correction for multiple testing or autocorrelation, which is the failure mode that negative-control calibration and FDR are meant to guard against. The only formal space-time analysis of flaps found is the qualitative or alignment-based literature (orthoteny). No Knox or similar contagion test of report clustering was located. Using these designs together appears to be a new methodological contribution for UAP data. The methods themselves are well established.

status_corrections.relationship: UAP/UFO report counts x regional seismic activity over time (Tectonic Strain Theory: monthly or yearly report counts vs earthquake counts, magnitudes or seismic energy, with lags)
status_corrections.reason: The hypothesis is well known, but the relationship is not established. All the positive correlations (Uinta r=0.80, Zeitoun r=0.56, Carman by visual inspection, New Madrid) come from one group (Persinger/Derr) in one journal, with post-hoc choices of radius (150 to 1000 km) and lag. Published critiques (Rutkowski 1984 thesis and Perceptual and Motor Skills 58:840-842; Rutkowski and Del Bigio 1989 CMAJ) remain unanswered, and I found no independent replication. The relationship's own summary says this. 'WELL KNOWN' implies an accepted finding, comparable to the established earthquake-light literature, which the evidence does not support. 'PREVIOUSLY SUGGESTED (published, contested, unreplicated)' is the accurate label.

status_corrections.relationship: UAP reports (especially radar/electronic and radar-visual cases) x ionospheric disturbance (sporadic-E, storm-time ionospheric irregularities, radar aurora, solar radio bursts)
status_corrections.reason: The qualitative mechanism has a UAP-specific precedent. Condon Report Section VI, Chapter 5, 'Radar and the Observation of UFOs' (Blackmer et al., 1968), has an 'Ionization phenomena' subsection. It says ionospheric layers and the aurora can produce radar echoes ('auroral echoes ... 60-180 mi ... mainly stationary ... usually in the magnetic north azimuths') that could be taken for UFOs. So the summary's statement that the Condon Report treated anomalous propagation only as tropospheric is wrong; that holds only for Section III, Chapter 5 (Thayer). What remains unprecedented is the quantitative test of radar-UAP report RATES against ionospheric indices (foEs, foF2, TEC, radio-burst days). Suggested label: PREVIOUSLY SUGGESTED (qualitative), with no quantitative precedent located.

status_corrections.relationship: UAP report counts (annual, regional) x lagged geomagnetic activity indices (Persinger's tectonic-strain regression models)
status_corrections.reason: The label stands, but the summary contains a factual error to fix. Medina et al. (2023) do NOT describe the tectonic-strain work as 'refuted soon after publication'. That phrase refers to the Uinta Basin insect / St. Elmo's-fire hypothesis. Medina cites the tectonic strain hypothesis neutrally and only notes that seismic activity is too rare to explain most reports. The evidence against Persinger's models rests on Rutkowski's critique and the lack of replication, not on Medina.

SEPRA's original 1989 'B' was 'phenomene naturel spectaculaire de propagation lumineuse', and it was the gendarmeries, not SEPRA, that linked it to the solar eruption. status_corrections.relationship: UAP report counts (and POSS-I plate transients) x dates of atmospheric nuclear tests, 1949-1957 (temporal)
status_corrections.reason: A peer-reviewed paper directly reports the UAP-report x test-date association, so this is more than a suggestion. Bruehl & Villarroel (2025, Sci Rep 15:34125) found 'Small but significant (p = .008) associations between nuclear testing and number of UAP reports' in the published version, not only the preprint. Treat it as contested and unreplicated: it is one group's result; Watters et al. (2026) explicitly do not address the UAP-report component or the continuous statistics; and Doherty (2026) replicates only the transient-test link. There is also an earlier precedent. Ruppelt (1956, Ch. 16) reports that Blue Book plotted sighting peaks against 'world-wide atomic tests' and 'could never say what caused' them, an informal null test. Correct the summary: 2,718 is calendar days, not POSS-I observation days. Transients occurred on 310 days, and Watters counts about 312 plate days.

status_corrections.relationship: UAP reports x proximity to nuclear-weapons infrastructure (atomic labs, weapons storage, ICBM fields), spatial and historical
status_corrections.reason: The label holds, but the summary is wrong that the 1950s USAF spatial analysis 'appears only in secondary accounts'. It is in Ruppelt's 1956 primary account, and its results were mixed. Ch. 9: Los Alamos-Albuquerque, Oak Ridge and White Sands 'rated high'. Ch. 16: 'Strategic Air Command and Air Defense Command bases, some A-bomb storage areas, and large military depots actually produced fewer reports than could be expected from a given area'. So the earliest crude, area-normalized USAF analysis contradicts a general excess near weapons storage and strategic bases, while supporting one near atomic-energy and test installations. Also, the Boeing/USAF 'electronic noise pulse' finding for Echo Flight is documented in Carlson's PDF, not in the cited Wikipedia article.
